courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: Pointwise, pairwise and listwise approaches
question: Query Q1 has 10 documents and query Q2 has 200, each with mixed labels. With an unnormalized pairwise loss, what goes wrong?
options: Nothing, because pairs are formed per query
Q1 dominates, because its pairs are more informative
Q2 dominates, because it can contribute vastly more pairs, so the loss stops tracking the per-query average NDCG
The model cannot be trained because pair counts differ
explain: Pair counts can grow quadratically with documents per query, so a few big queries dominate a pairwise loss. Liu describes query-level normalization (dividing by the query's pair count) as the fix; LightGBM, a gradient boosting library covered in the final lesson, also normalizes per query with lambdarank_norm.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: Dropping the softmax turns attention into an RNN
question: A linear-attention layer with $d_k=d_v=128$ per head has generated 10,000 tokens. What does it need to keep per head to generate token 10,001?
options: All 10,000 keys and values, like a KV cache
The 128 x 128 state matrix S
Only the last 128 keys
The full 10,000 x 10,000 attention matrix
explain: Everything the layer knows about the past is folded into $S_t$, a 128 x 128 matrix (16,384 numbers) regardless of how many tokens came before. That is the RNN view of linear attention.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: Three ways to compute one layer: parallel, recurrent, chunkwise
question: You must train a Gated DeltaNet layer on 8K-token sequences on GPUs. Which computation form should the training kernel use?
options: Recurrent form, because it has the fewest FLOPs
Fully parallel form, because it has no sequential steps
Chunkwise form, which keeps FLOPs near linear and turns most work into matmuls with only L/C sequential steps
Any form, they run equally fast
explain: The recurrent form serializes 8K small updates and cannot use tensor cores well; the parallel form pays $O(L^2d)$ FLOPs. Chunkwise is what FLA and the paper use for training.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: Decoding, serving and hybrid models in production
question: Qwen3-Next's context grows from 32K to 256K tokens. Which part of its per-sequence cache grows?
options: Only the KV cache of the 12 full-attention layers; the Gated DeltaNet state stays 72 MiB
Only the Gated DeltaNet state
Both grow 8x
Neither grows
explain: Gated DeltaNet layers keep a fixed $d_k\times d_v$ state per head regardless of length. The attention layers' KV cache grows linearly: 768 MiB at 32K to 6,144 MiB at 256K, while the 72 MiB state is unchanged.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Setuid, setgid and sticky: borrowed privilege and its bugs
question: In /tmp (mode 1777), user bob tries to delete /tmp/alice-upload.zip, which alice owns. What happens?
options: It fails, because the sticky bit allows only the file's owner, the directory's owner or root to delete it
It works, because /tmp is writable by everyone
It works only if the file's mode allows bob to write
It fails, because /tmp is owned by root
explain: Write permission on a directory normally allows deleting any entry. The sticky bit (the 1 in 1777) narrows that to the file's owner, the directory's owner and privileged processes, so bob is refused.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Packages and updates, and the xz-utils backdoor
question: What tipped off Andres Freund to the xz backdoor?
options: An antivirus alert
SSH logins using unusual CPU time and running slower, plus valgrind errors
A CVE published by the attacker
A failed package signature check
explain: No security tool flagged it. A developer noticed sshd taking about half a second longer and memory-checker errors, and refused to ignore the anomaly.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: What an intruder touches: persistence and where defenders look
question: Which check would catch an intruder who copied /bin/bash to /var/tmp/.x and set the setuid bit (owner root)?
options: Listing /etc/systemd/system
A setuid file search compared with a baseline
journalctl -u ssh
Checking /etc/passwd for UID 0
explain: The new file is a root-owned setuid program that gives a root shell on demand. A find -perm -4000 diffed against a baseline shows a new setuid file, provided the search covers every mounted filesystem (-xdev stops at mount points, so run it per mount).

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Automating a benchmark: SCAP, OpenSCAP and ComplianceAsCode
question: Why does the exit status of `oscap xccdf eval` matter for fleet automation?
options: A script can branch on it (0 versus 2 in our runs) without parsing the text report
It encrypts the results file
It tells the kernel to reboot
It sets the profile level
explain: Machine-readable signals (the exit status, and res.xml) let a CI job, a cron wrapper or an agent mark a host non-compliant automatically. Parsing the human report is fragile.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: The Linux audit system: how a system call becomes a record
question: Why should pam_loginuid not be added to the PAM stack of sudo?
options: It would slow sudo down
sudo does not use PAM
It would disable auditd
sudo would set the login uid to the target account (root), erasing the record of who actually logged in
explain: Its manual says to use it only at entry points (login, sshd, cron) because on su or sudo it would change the loginuid to the account switched to, which "defeats the purpose".

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Tetragon: filtering and enforcing inside the kernel
question: A Tetragon policy sends Sigkill when a process writes to /etc/passwd via a hook on the write path. An analyst says the file can no longer be modified. What is the gap?
options: Tetragon cannot watch /etc
Sigkill only works in Kubernetes
The write is blocked but no event is generated
SIGKILL ends the process, but per the docs it does not guarantee the write did not happen; add Override to make the call fail
explain: The enforcement docs are explicit: a SIGKILL during write() does not guarantee the data is not written. Override makes the checked function return an error so the operation is not performed.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Case: Kinsing and TeamTNT, cryptominers on exposed Linux hosts
question: Which single prevention would have stopped the Kinsing PostgreSQL route Microsoft described?
options: Disabling io_uring
Not exposing the database to the internet and not using `trust` authentication for remote connections
Using `trust` authentication only for 0.0.0.0/0
Running PostgreSQL with MemoryDenyWriteExecute
explain: With trust authentication anyone who can connect is accepted as any user, including superusers. Remove internet exposure and require real authentication; the other options do not touch that door.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a fleet plan, and where to practise
question: You can do only one thing this quarter for a 2,000-host fleet with no automation. Which gives the most risk reduction per effort, based on this course's cases?
options: Write custom Tetragon enforcement policies for every service
Build a package inventory and an automated, ring-based patch pipeline that verifies running versions
Move every host to an immutable OS
Apply CIS Level 2 to every host at once
explain: Every case here needed either 'who is affected' answered fast or a patch applied everywhere, and inventory plus patching underpins the rest. Level 2 everywhere at once risks outages; immutable images and custom enforcement are later steps.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: From labels to leaderboards: do system rankings survive?
question: Per-topic tau in the TREC 2024 RAG study (0.553 for nDCG@20) is much lower than run-level tau (0.890). What does that tell you?
options: The LLM labels are useless
Run-level averages are wrong
LLM labels are noisy for any single query, so per-query diagnosis needs more care than leaderboard ranking
Per-topic tau is always lower because of a formula error
explain: Within one topic, label disagreements reorder runs a lot; averaged over 27 topics the noise cancels. Use LLM labels confidently for aggregate comparisons, cautiously for statements about a single query.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: BLEU, ROUGE and BERTScore, and where they fail
question: In the BERTScore toy, the reference token "sick" and candidate token "ill" have similarity 0.99. Which statement is true?
options: BERTScore recall counts "sick" as fully unmatched
BERTScore requires the candidate and reference to have equal length
BERTScore is identical to ROUGE-1 when idf weighting is off
BERTScore gives partial credit for paraphrases, but it would also give near-full credit to many factual swaps
explain: Greedy embedding matching rewards meaning-similar words, fixing the paraphrase problem. It does not verify facts, and words of the same type (weekdays, names, numbers) can be close in embedding space.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: Task-specific eval sets, regression tests and significance
question: Why is the paired interval (-0.02 to +0.22) narrower than the unpaired one (-0.08 to +0.28) on the same data?
options: Pairing uses more resamples
Pairing keeps each item's old and new result together, so item difficulty, which affects both versions, cancels out of the difference
The unpaired method has a bug
Pairing drops the items where both versions pass
explain: Most items are easy or hard for both versions. Resampling them together removes that shared variation from the difference; resampling separately adds it back as noise.

courseTitle: Guardrails for LLM applications
lessonTitle: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails: policies, strengths and grounding
question: Which denied-topic definition follows the AWS best practices?
options: Block all content about crypto
Everything except checking and savings accounts
Any message that mentions the competitor name ExampleBank
Questions or information about investing, selling, transacting or procuring cryptocurrencies
explain: The docs ask for a crisp definition of the subject. The first is an instruction, the second a negative definition, and the third targets a word, which belongs in a word filter.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Measuring a server: latency percentiles, load curves and benchmarks
question: Two configurations have the same mean TPOT, 30 ms. Configuration X has a p99 ITL of 40 ms, configuration Y of 450 ms. Which statement is most likely?
options: Y uses a larger token budget, so some steps carry big prefill chunks that stall every decode in them
X uses a larger token budget
Y has a smaller KV pool
The two are equivalent for users, since TPOT is the same
explain: Equal averages with very different tails point to occasional long steps. A large budget lets a step carry thousands of prompt tokens, and every decoding request in that step waits for it. TPOT averages those stalls away; the ITL tail shows them.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: When the pool runs dry: admission control and preemption
question: Spot the bug: a scheduler allocates blocks on demand, admits a new request whenever its prompt's blocks are free, and has no preemption code. What eventually happens under heavy load?
options: Running requests need new blocks that are not there, so the step cannot proceed: an out-of-memory failure or a deadlock
Nothing, block allocation can never fail
Throughput drops but every request still finishes
Requests are silently truncated to their prompt length and returned
explain: On-demand allocation without a fallback is exactly the deadlock Orca's reservation avoids: every running request may need one more block at the same moment. You need either worst-case reservation or preemption with swap or recompute.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: Few-shot examples and asking the model to reason first
question: Your sentiment prompt has four examples, all labeled positive, and the model now labels most neutral reviews positive. What is the most likely cause?
options: Four examples are too few for in-context learning
The examples are not diverse, so the model picked up 'answer positive' as part of the pattern
Examples only affect format, never labels
The model needs gradient updates to learn labels
explain: Examples teach whatever pattern they share, intended or not. Anthropic's advice is to make examples diverse and to cover edge cases. Brown et al. show that examples steer behavior with no gradient updates at all.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: Validation, retries and the pitfalls of strict formats
question: A summarization job uses a strict schema with max_tokens set to 200. About 3 percent of replies fail to parse even though constrained decoding is on. What is the most likely cause?
options: The decoder's mask has a bug that lets invalid tokens through
Those replies hit the 200-token limit and were cut off mid-JSON
The model refused, which always produces invalid JSON
JSON Schema cannot describe summaries
explain: A mask keeps every prefix valid and allows stopping only at an accept state, but the token limit cuts generation off regardless. Check the stop reason (max_tokens or incomplete) and raise the limit or shorten the output.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Latency budgets, caching and parallel fallback
question: Which cache key is safest for storing parsed filter objects?
options: The raw query string exactly as typed
The normalized query string alone
The normalized query plus the user's session ID
The normalized query plus the schema version and vocabulary version
explain: Raw strings fragment the cache on case and spacing. Without versions, a schema or dictionary change keeps serving stale parses (an old field name, a city ID that was split). The session ID would make the cache nearly useless, since the parse does not depend on who asked.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Cutting decode: FIRST and single-token listwise ranking
question: At k=100, L=100, w=20, FIRST brings our modeled query latency from 10.35 s to 2.39 s. Which next change cuts FIRST's latency the most?
options: Raising the window step s while keeping w = 20, which removes windows and their prefill
Asking for a shorter permutation format
Using a higher sampling temperature
Adding a reasoning step before the ranking
explain: FIRST has no permutation to shorten, so the remaining time is prefill on a chain of windows. Fewer windows (or fewer tokens per window) is what is left. A reasoning step would add decode tokens back.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Pointwise: yes/no relevance and query likelihood
question: Your API returns only generated text, no log-probabilities. Which pointwise method can you still run, and with what limitation?
options: Query likelihood, because it uses teacher forcing
Neither; pointwise prompts cannot work without fine-tuning
Yes/No generation, but you only get a binary label, so many passages tie and the ranking is coarse
Both, as long as you set temperature to 0
explain: Query likelihood needs the probability of the given query tokens, which a text-only API cannot provide. Yes/No still produces an answer, but without p(Yes) you only get two buckets, so passages inside a bucket keep their original order.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Position bias, robustness and distilled rerankers
question: Your listwise reranker works well on BM25 input but degrades badly when you switch the first stage to a new retriever that returns candidates in a near-random order. Which fix targets the cause?
options: Increase the window step so fewer windows are needed
Lower the temperature to 0
Shuffle the input several times and aggregate the rankings, or use a student trained with shuffled inputs
Switch to query likelihood, which is order-free but needs no changes
explain: The symptom is order sensitivity: failures and the one-pass guarantee both lean on a good initial order. Permutation self-consistency marginalizes the order out, and RankVicuna/RankZephyr train on shuffled inputs for the same reason. Temperature 0 makes outputs repeatable, not order-invariant.

courseTitle: LLM routing and cascades: cheap model or strong model
lessonTitle: Deferral signals: when should a cascade escalate?
question: In AutoMix's setting, why might a router decline to escalate a query whose self-verification confidence is very low?
options: Because the meta-verifier has learned that such queries are often unsolvable by any model, so paying for the large model would not improve the answer
Because low confidence always means the small model is right
Because escalation is disabled for low scores by default
Because the verifier's samples are too expensive to repeat
explain: The meta-verifier reasons about hidden states. If very low confidence mostly comes from queries no model can answer, escalating them spends money without gaining accuracy. Middle confidence, which more often comes from queries the large model can fix, is where escalation pays.

courseTitle: LLM routing and cascades: cheap model or strong model
lessonTitle: Build and run a router in production
question: A chat product routes every turn independently and sends 40% of turns to the strong model. Its input-token bill is about the same as sending every turn to the strong model. What is the most likely cause?
options: The router's scores are miscalibrated
Output tokens are counted as input tokens
Switching models between turns discards each model's cached conversation prefix, so every switch re-processes the whole history at full (cache write) price
The weak model is more expensive per token
explain: Prompt caching is per model. With caching, staying on one model pays about 0.1x for the long history on each turn; a switch pays 1.25x for all the history the other model has not cached yet. Route per conversation, or pin conversations to a model (session affinity) and re-route only when the context is short.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: RANSAC: keeping only matches that agree on one homography
question: findHomography returns an H that maps the book cover to the wrong place, with only 6 inliers out of 300 matches. What is the most likely cause?
options: The inlier ratio is so low that 2000 iterations never drew a clean sample, often because matching was too loose or the object is absent
The reprojection threshold is too large
RANSAC always fails for homographies
The homography needs 8 points, not 4
explain: With 2% inliers, a clean 4-point sample has probability 0.02^4 = 1.6e-7 per draw, so 2000 iterations almost never find one, and the best random model wins with a handful of accidental inliers. Tighten the ratio test, check the object is visible, or require a minimum inlier count before trusting H.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: The Michael-Scott queue: a dummy node and helping
question: Why does a dequeuer at D6 check `head.ptr == tail.ptr` and, if the queue is non-empty, advance Tail before moving Head?
options: To keep Tail from ever pointing at a dequeued node, so dequeued nodes can be safely reused
Because Head and Tail must always be equal
To save one CAS in enqueue
Because Tail must be moved under a lock
explain: The paper: the dequeue ensures Tail does not point to the dequeued node or any predecessor, which is what lets dequeued nodes be reused. Valois's earlier algorithm let Tail lag behind Head and could not safely free nodes for exactly this reason.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: Spell: templates from the longest common subsequence
question: The prefix tree holds templates DA and ABC, and the line DAPBC arrives. The paper notes the prefix tree returns DA here rather than ABC. Why is that approximation acceptable in Spell?
options: DA is the correct answer: it is the longest template that is a subsequence of DAPBC
A subsequence match is unique, so DA must be the only candidate
Returning DA is a bug that Spell fixes by always falling back to the exhaustive loop
The walk is greedy from the root, so it takes the first matching path; that is almost always right because parameters sit near the end of a line, and the full loop runs when it finds nothing
explain: The prefix tree guarantees only that it returns some template that is a subsequence, not the longest. Spell accepts the approximation because parameters cluster near the end of log lines, and it measured a 100 percent agreement with the exhaustive loop on a 433,490-record HPC log. When the prefilter finds nothing, fewer than 0.1 percent of lines, the full search runs with a Jaccard screen first.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Why log at all, and why not log everything
question: A team keeps 14 days of searchable logs. An intrusion is discovered 60 days after it began. Which question can they still answer from their logs?
options: What the intruder did in the last two weeks
How the intruder first got in
Every account the intruder touched
Nothing at all, logs older than 14 days corrupt the rest
explain: Only the most recent 14 days survive, so they can describe recent activity but not the way in or the full scope. That gap is why retention is set from expected dwell time (how long intruders stay unnoticed).

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: The pipeline: collect, ship, parse, enrich, store
question: Why does a pipeline put a buffer or queue between agents and the SIEM?
options: So events wait instead of being lost when the SIEM is slow or down
To encrypt events
To remove duplicate events
To convert XML to JSON
explain: Without a buffer, an outage or a burst larger than the indexer can absorb drops events, and dropped events are invisible by definition.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: MITRE ATT&CK as a coverage map
question: Your coverage map shows three rules tagged T1098.005 (Device Registration). Which fact would most change your confidence?
options: None has been tested end to end, and the identity provider's registration events are not ingested
All three are severity high
They were written by different people
They use different query languages
explain: Untested rules over missing data detect nothing, whatever the map says. Coverage claims need data and tests behind them.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Correlation and sequence rules: Uber 2022 and MFA fatigue
question: One IP address fails to log in once each to 300 different accounts in 20 minutes. Which Sigma correlation type fits best?
options: event_count grouped by user
temporal_ordered
value_count of user grouped by source IP
No correlation needed, one failure is enough
explain: Password spraying is few attempts per account but many distinct accounts per source. Counting distinct user values per source IP catches it; counting events per user (1 each) never would.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Position Interpolation and NTK-aware scaling
question: A Llama 2 model (L = 4096) is extended with PI to 16,384 tokens. What position value does RoPE receive for the token at index 10,000?
options: 4,096, clipped to the trained maximum
explain: s = 16384 / 4096 = 4, and PI feeds m / s = 10000 / 4 = 2500. Positions are scaled, not clipped; fractional values are allowed.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Hiding communication, causal balance and Ulysses
question: Ring Attention with 4 ranks and contiguous chunks shows rank 3 at full utilization and rank 0 mostly idle on a causal model. Which change fixes this without changing the math?
options: Increase the block size c
Assign each rank tokens or chunks spread across the sequence (striped or zigzag)
Switch to bidirectional attention
Reduce the number of KV heads
explain: The imbalance comes from the causal triangle: later query chunks attend to more keys. Striped Attention or Llama 3's chunk i plus chunk 2CP - 1 - i assignment gives every rank the same amount of unmasked work.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: What a loop can compute: algorithms, latent thoughts, fixed points
question: Which update is path independent, converging to the same state from every start?
explain: 0.5 s + e halves the distance to its fixed point 2e every step, so every start converges there. s + e keeps adding (the start is never forgotten), 2s + e doubles the distance and diverges, and s = s keeps whatever it started with.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Spending compute at test time: more loops, early exits, shared caches
question: Using the paper's description (a budget counted in iterations, k = 16), Huginn keeps 16 cache slots per token. Which slot does iteration 33 write, and whose entry does it replace?
options: Slot 1, replacing iteration 17
Slot 0, replacing iteration 32
Slot 1, replacing iteration 1 only
Slot 33, because each iteration gets a new slot
explain: 33 mod 16 = 1. Slot 1 was written by iteration 1, overwritten by iteration 17, and is now overwritten by iteration 33. That a token can read entries written at other depths is what Huginn's MT-Bench runs support empirically; it is not guaranteed for every looped model.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: LoRA: a frozen weight plus a trainable low-rank update
question: A colleague initializes both A and B to zero to be extra safe. What happens during training?
options: Training proceeds normally but more slowly
A learns first, then B
The update stays exactly zero, because each matrix's gradient is multiplied by the other matrix
The model diverges because the scale alpha/r is applied to zeros
explain: The gradient for B contains Ax and the gradient for A contains B. With both at zero, both gradients are zero at every step, so nothing ever changes. That is why one of the two must be random.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: The wider PEFT family, and when LoRA falls short
question: A team wants to teach Llama-2-7B a new programming language by training on 20B tokens of raw source code, and to keep its English skills. What does the evidence suggest?
options: LoRA at r = 16 will match full fine-tuning and forget nothing
Full fine-tuning will likely learn the domain better, while LoRA preserves more of the base skills; pick based on which matters more
Prompt tuning is the best choice because it has the fewest parameters
Rank does not matter in continued pretraining
explain: In Biderman et al.'s continued pretraining runs, full fine-tuning outperformed every LoRA rank on the target domain, and LoRA forgot less. That is a real tradeoff, not a free lunch, and rank clearly ordered LoRA's results.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Exact unlearning: retraining without the data, made cheaper with SISA
question: A SISA system with S = 20 shards batches 60 uniformly random deletion requests before retraining. Roughly what fraction of the shard models must be retrained?
options: About 95%, almost every shard is hit at least once
About 5%, one shard per batch
About 33%, since 60 / 20 = 3 requests per shard on average
100% exactly, because 60 is larger than 20
explain: Each shard escapes all 60 requests with probability (1 - 1/20)^60, about 0.046, so about 95.4% of shards are hit at least once. It is not exactly 100% because some shards can get zero requests by chance. This saturation is why SISA's measured speed-ups shrink as requests pile up.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Measuring forgetting: TOFU, MUSE and the forget-retain tradeoff
question: Why does TOFU aggregate its nine utility numbers with a harmonic mean rather than an arithmetic mean?
options: It is faster to compute
So that one collapsed ability drags the score down instead of being averaged away
Because the metrics have different units
So that utility is always at least 0.5
explain: A harmonic mean is dominated by its smallest inputs. In the example, one score dropping to 0.02 moves the arithmetic mean only to 0.724 but the harmonic mean to 0.150. The TOFU authors chose it for exactly this reason: they did not want low scores to be averaged out.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: Code signing: what a signature on a Mac proves
question: A binary shows `Signature=adhoc` and `TeamIdentifier=not set`. What can you conclude?
options: It was notarized by Apple
Its pages match the stored hashes, but no certificate ties it to any developer
It is an Apple platform binary
It cannot run on Apple silicon
explain: Ad hoc means integrity without identity: the Code Directory hashes exist, but nothing is signed with a certificate. Apple silicon accepts ad hoc signatures for running locally, so it can run; it just tells you nothing about who made it.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: SIP and the signed system volume: root is not enough
question: Malware gains root on a Mac with SIP enabled and tries to replace `/usr/bin/sudo`. What happens?
options: It succeeds, because root can write anywhere
It succeeds only if the Mac has no FileVault
macOS asks the user for permission
The write is denied: SIP applies to every process, including root
explain: Apple's SIP page: the policy applies regardless of administrative privileges. /usr is also on the read-only signed system volume. Root malware has to go through an entitled Apple process or a bug, as Shrootless did.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: Persistence on macOS: launchd, login items and BTM
question: A stealer has no admin password. Which persistence location is it most likely to use?
options: ~/Library/LaunchAgents
/Library/LaunchDaemons
/System/Library/LaunchAgents
/usr/libexec
explain: The per-user LaunchAgents folder is writable by the user. /Library needs admin rights, and /System and /usr are on the sealed, SIP-protected system volume.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: Managing a Mac fleet: MDM, profiles and declarative management
question: A user on a supervised, Automated-Device-Enrolled Mac runs `sudo profiles remove` on the MDM enrollment profile. What does Apple's documentation say happens?
options: Removal is prevented, both from System Settings and from the profiles tool
It succeeds, since the user is an admin
The Mac is wiped
Only FileVault is turned off
explain: Prevent unenrollment applies to supervised devices and blocks removal from System Settings and from the profiles command-line tool. That is why organisation-owned Macs should use Automated Device Enrollment.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: A Mac hardening baseline, and where to practise
question: Your fleet report says 4% of Macs show `SIP: disabled`. What is the right first response?
options: Ignore it: SIP is only for developers
Turn off Gatekeeper on those Macs
Treat each as a finding: identify why (developer exception or tampering), re-enable via recoveryOS, and check those Macs for kernel extensions or system modifications
Delete the MDM profile
explain: SIP can only be turned off from recoveryOS, so each case is a deliberate action by someone with physical or admin access. Some are legitimate developer exceptions; all need an owner and a check.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: The PE format: headers, sections and what imports reveal
question: A DLL's import table lists only LoadLibraryA and GetProcAddress from KERNEL32. What is the most reasonable next step?
options: Suspect run-time import resolution (often packing) and look at entropy and dynamic behaviour
Conclude it is harmless because it imports almost nothing
Delete the import table and rerun pefile
Trust the TimeDateStamp to date the sample
explain: A real program needs many OS functions. Importing only the two that load others suggests it builds its import list at run time, which packers and obfuscated malware do. Check section entropy and watch it run.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Dynamic analysis: sandboxes, monitors and the WannaCry kill switch
question: In Mandiant's analysis, what made WannaCry exit immediately?
options: A successful InternetOpenUrl request to its hard-coded domain
Finding antivirus running
Running on Windows XP
The presence of a mutex
explain: If the request to the hard-coded domain succeeded, the malware exited. Registering the domain made it succeed everywhere the sample could reach it.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Indicators of compromise and the Pyramid of Pain
question: Per Bianco, what does detecting a distinctive User-Agent string from an attacker's tool force the attacker to do?
options: Nothing; they just switch IP address
Abandon their entire operation
Register new domains
Go back to their lab and reconfigure or recompile the tool
explain: Network and host artifacts sit in the middle of the pyramid: denying them costs the attacker real rework, unlike changing an IP or a hash.

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: Storage math: dimensions times bytes per number
question: You store 10M vectors from text-embedding-3-large. Option 1: 3072-d float32. Option 2: 1024-d int8. How much smaller is option 2?
options: 3x
4x
explain: Option 1: 3072 x 4 = 12,288 bytes per vector (122.88 GB). Option 2: 1024 x 1 = 1,024 bytes (10.24 GB). The ratio is 3 (dims) x 4 (bytes) = 12.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, CP, MoE, FP8 and MFU
lessonTitle: Tensor parallelism: column and row splits of the MLP and attention
question: In a 2-way TP MLP, an engineer splits the first weight matrix A by rows instead of columns, keeping everything else the same. What breaks?
options: Nothing, matrix multiplication is linear so the split does not matter
GeLU is applied to partial sums, so outputs are wrong unless an extra all-reduce is inserted before the GeLU
The backward pass needs twice as much memory
The second GEMM can no longer be split
explain: A row split of A gives each GPU a partial pre-activation. GeLU is nonlinear, so GeLU of the parts does not add up to GeLU of the whole (1.683 vs 1.954 in the example). The column split avoids this synchronization entirely.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, CP, MoE, FP8 and MFU
lessonTitle: Context parallelism: balanced causal splits and the KV ring
question: A model has 64 query heads and 8 KV heads and trains with TP = 4 and CP = 4 at 32K tokens. Which `--cp-comm-type` will Transformer Engine reject?
options: a2a, because each GPU holds only 2 KV heads and 2 is not divisible by CP = 4
p2p, because the ring needs the sequence to be divisible by 64
allgather, because it cannot be combined with TP
None of them; any type works with grouped-query attention
explain: a2a scatters heads across the CP group, so the per-GPU query heads (64 / 4 = 16) and KV heads (8 / 4 = 2) must both be divisible by CP. 2 is not divisible by 4. p2p only needs the sequence divisible by 2 x CP = 8; a2a+p2p with an a2a group of 2 would also work.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, CP, MoE, FP8 and MFU
lessonTitle: Measuring the result: MFU, HFU and what the numbers count
question: Two runs of the same model on the same GPUs both report 160 TFLOP/s per GPU. Run A uses full recompute, run B uses selective recompute. Which trains faster in tokens per second?
options: Run A, because full recompute frees memory for larger batches
They are the same, the TFLOP/s are equal
Run B, because fewer of its FLOPs are wasted on recomputation, so more go to useful model FLOPs
It cannot be decided without knowing the vocabulary size
explain: Both execute FLOPs at the same rate, but A spends about a quarter of them redoing the forward pass. B's model FLOPs per second, and so its MFU and tokens per second, are higher. This is exactly the HFU vs MFU distinction.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Acquiring RAM: WinPmem, DumpIt, LiME, AVML and virtual machines
question: You must capture RAM from a VMware guest you suspect has a kernel rootkit. Which option runs no code inside the guest?
options: Run WinPmem inside the guest
Copy the guest's pagefile from inside Windows
Take a disk snapshot of the guest's virtual disk
Suspend or snapshot the VM and collect the .vmem with its .vmss or .vmsn file from the host
explain: The hypervisor holds the guest's RAM and can save it without the guest's cooperation. A disk snapshot has no RAM, and anything run inside the guest is exposed to the rootkit.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Know normal: the process tree, command lines and the PEB
question: ldrmodules shows a memory region mapping a DLL file that is absent from all three loader lists. What does that suggest?
options: The DLL may have been loaded or hidden outside the normal loader, so investigate the region and its file
The DLL is a normal system DLL and can be ignored
The image is from Linux
The process exited before capture
explain: The normal loader records each DLL in its lists. A file-backed mapping with no list entries means something bypassed or edited them: unlink-to-hide and manual mapping both look like this.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Credential artefacts: what memory exposes and how to scope it
question: A host had Credential Guard enabled. Which statement matches Microsoft's documentation?
options: NTLM hashes and Kerberos TGTs are isolated in LSAIso.exe, but credentials typed for NTLM authentication and Kerberos service tickets are not protected
All credentials of every kind are removed from memory
Credential Guard has no effect on LSASS
Credential Guard stores passwords on disk instead of in memory
explain: Credential Guard narrows exposure; it does not eliminate it. Scope still includes service tickets and anything typed in, so resets and monitoring remain necessary.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Anti-forensics against memory analysis, and the cross-view answer
question: Which capture method gives the best chance against a kernel rootkit that interferes with acquisition inside a virtual machine?
options: Running the same acquisition tool twice inside the guest
Copying the guest's pagefile
Rebooting the guest into safe mode first
Taking the guest's memory from the hypervisor, outside the guest
explain: The hypervisor holds the guest's RAM and does not depend on the guest's kernel. Rebooting destroys the evidence; inside-guest tools can be interfered with.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Placement policy: where a block goes decides what survives
question: A program allocates objects from 16 bytes to 128 KiB. A colleague says Robson's bound proves it will use 13x its live memory. What is wrong?
options: Nothing; the bound applies to every program with that size range
Robson's bound only applies to garbage-collected languages
The bound is a worst case over adversarial sequences; real traces with good policies were near 0%
The bound is log base 10, so it is about 4x
explain: Robson's result says some request sequence can force that blow-up on any non-moving allocator. It does not say typical programs reach it. Johnstone and Wilson measured near-zero fragmentation for good policies on real programs.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: Acquire and release: publishing data across threads
question: In `get_data`, someone changes the compare_exchange failure ordering from Acquire to Relaxed. What can go wrong?
options: Nothing, because failure means no store happened, so ordering is irrelevant
The losing thread uses the winner's pointer without synchronizing with the Release that published it, so it may read uninitialized Data
The compare_exchange may now succeed twice
It only affects performance on x86
explain: On failure the operation still loads the winner's pointer, and that pointer is then dereferenced. Without Acquire on that load there is no happens-before from the winner's initialization, so the read of Data is a data race. Mara Bos uses Acquire for exactly this reason.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Why freeing a removed node is the hard part
question: Which threads can possibly hold a reference to a node that was unlinked at time t?
options: Any thread that will run in the future
Only the thread that unlinked it
Only threads whose current operation started before t and is still running
No thread, because unlinking is atomic
explain: After the unlink, the node is unreachable from shared memory, so an operation starting later cannot find it. Only operations already in progress at time t may have loaded its address. Every scheme here is a way to detect when those operations have finished, or that they do not point at this node.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Choosing a scheme: read cost versus bounded garbage
question: A kernel subsystem keeps a routing table read millions of times per second and updated a few times per minute. Readers never sleep while holding entries. What is the best choice?
options: Hazard pointers on every table entry
A reader-writer lock
Reference counting each entry
RCU: readers use rcu_read_lock, updaters publish a copy and free with call_rcu or kfree_rcu
explain: This is RCU's design point: read-mostly data, non-sleeping readers and natural quiescent states. Readers make no shared writes, while hazard pointers would fence per visited entry and a reader-writer lock makes every reader write to the lock word. Rare updates make the grace-period wait cheap.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Heap overflow: corrupting the neighbouring object
question: Why did the 17-character note make ana an admin even though no code assigned is_admin?
options: The 17th byte was written one past the note's block, which on this allocator is the first byte of is_admin
strcpy writes a full 32-byte line whatever the input length
malloc put is_admin inside the note's own 16 bytes
The session was freed and given to the note
explain: The overflow wrote into memory the program never meant to touch, and that memory belonged to the session. Nothing assigned is_admin; its bytes were overwritten as a side effect.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Use-after-free and double free: dangling pointers
question: In CVE-2019-13720, which change removes the bug?
options: Set reverb_ to null right after freeing it in SetBuffer
Make reverb_ a global so it is never freed early
Take the same lock in SetBuffer that Process() holds, before freeing reverb_
Check in Process() whether reverb_ is null before each use, without a lock
explain: The two threads disagreed about who may touch reverb_ and when. With both sides holding process_lock_, the free cannot happen while Process() is using the object. Nulling the pointer or checking it without the lock still leaves a window where one thread frees while the other is mid-use.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Why memory-safe languages remove whole bug classes
question: According to the Android data, what most reduced Android's share of memory safety vulnerabilities?
options: Rewriting all old C++ in Rust
Turning on AddressSanitizer in production
Writing most new code in memory-safe languages while leaving existing C++ in place
Removing the media library
explain: Google's 2022 post says the goal was not to convert existing C/C++ but to shift new development to memory-safe languages. As new unsafe code shrank, the share of memory safety bugs fell from 76 to 35 percent.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Measuring re-ID: rank-1, mAP, the Market-1501 protocol, re-ranking
question: System X ranks a query's 10 true matches at positions 1, 40, 41, ..., 48. System Y ranks them at positions 2 to 11. Which statement is right?
options: X has the better rank-1 and the better AP
Both have the same AP because both find all 10 matches
Y has the better rank-1, X the better AP
X has the better rank-1, but Y has a much better AP
explain: X's first match is at position 1, so rank-1 is a hit for X and a miss for Y. But X buries 9 matches around position 40, so its precision at those hits is low. AP is about 0.22 for X and 0.80 for Y. AP rewards finding all instances early, which is why Market-1501 reports mAP.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: Noise, repetitions and when a difference is real
question: Version X averages 102 ns with 95% interval [98, 106]. Version Y averages 100 ns with interval [97, 103]. What should you conclude?
options: Y is 2% faster; ship it
X is faster because its interval is wider
Compare the fastest runs instead
The data do not show a difference; reduce noise or take more runs before deciding
explain: The intervals overlap heavily, so a 2 ns gap is within what noise produces. Width says how uncertain the mean is, not which version is faster. The best-of approach is the misleading method that Georges et al. warn against.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Token-in-token-out: train on the tokens you actually sampled
question: A harness re-serializes tool-call arguments (same JSON object, different whitespace) on every turn. Under the strict matcher, a linear session keeps rolling back. What is the narrowest fix the docs offer?
options: --session-message-matcher loose_tool_call
--session-message-matcher role_content_only
Pass --apply-chat-template so the harness renders the prompt
Set input_ids yourself in each request
explain: loose_tool_call accepts equivalent JSON-object argument representations while still requiring call IDs, function names and order to match. role_content_only would also work but can merge genuinely different tool histories. The docs say not to apply the chat template manually or set TITO control fields like input_ids.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Moving a trillion parameters, and surviving dead engines
question: You train GLM-5 (744B) with 16 nodes per side and weight sync is eating about a minute per step. Which change matches the measurements in the docs?
options: Keep broadcast but double --update-weight-buffer-size; P2P only helps dense models
Use --colocate; the transfer then becomes P2P automatically
Switch to --update-weight-transfer-mode p2p; it cut GLM-5 updates from 58.3 s to 8.5 s
Switch to P2P only if you run on a single node
explain: The measured GLM-5 update fell 85.5% with P2P at 16 nodes per side. P2P's advantage grows with fleet width and is largest on MoE models, where expert parallelism cuts per-target data. On a single node it was slower. Colocated runs hand weights over locally, with no transport.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: LRB: learning to evict like a relaxed Belady
question: The boundary is 1M requests. Which training target choice best fits what LRB needs to get right?
options: log(time to next request), so the error between 100K and 2M counts more than between 2M and 3M
Raw time to next request with L2 loss, so large values dominate the loss
A binary label, recently used or not
The number of past requests
explain: The model only has to decide which side of the boundary an object falls on and rank the candidates. On a log scale a 20x error near the boundary is large while a 1.5x error far beyond it is small. The paper tried raw time, binary classification and other targets; log time gave the highest good decision ratio.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: Inside an APK and an IPA: what anyone can download and read
question: You copy an App Store app's main binary from a jailbroken iPhone and open it in a disassembler, but the code section looks like random bytes. What is the most likely reason?
options: iOS binaries are compressed with ZIP
Swift code cannot be disassembled
The app is obfuscated by default by Xcode
App Store binaries are encrypted with Apple's DRM, so a decrypted copy must be dumped from memory while the app runs, or obtained from the developer
explain: The MASTG notes that because of DRM the binary is encrypted when stored on the device; pulling it from the bundle is not enough. The IPA is a ZIP, but the binary inside it is the encrypted part. Xcode does not obfuscate by default, and Swift binaries disassemble like any other.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: Android IPC: exported components, intent redirection, PendingIntents
question: Why did the EngageSDK flaw affect apps whose developers never wrote an exported activity?
options: Because Android exports every activity by default since Android 12
Because the SDK modified the app's code at runtime
Because the library's own manifest added an exported activity to each app's merged manifest during the build
Because Google Play exports components after upload
explain: Microsoft explains that MTCommonActivity was added to the merged manifest when the library was imported, appearing only after the build, which is why developers missed it. Android 12 made the exported attribute mandatory for components with intent filters; it did not export everything.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: The app is not the boundary: backend APIs seen through the app
question: A tester toggles 'hide my age' in a dating app, then checks their own profile through the proxy from a second test account. The screen shows no age, but the JSON has `"birth_year": 1994`. How should this be reported?
options: As server-side excessive data exposure: the API ignores the privacy setting and sends the field anyway
Not a finding, since the app hides it correctly
As a client-side rendering bug to be fixed in the app
As a certificate pinning failure, because the proxy could read it
explain: The setting must be enforced where the data leaves the server; any client, including a script, receives the field. It is OWASP API3 (Broken Object Property Level Authorization, its excessive data exposure half) and a MASVS-PRIVACY concern. The proxy only made it visible; the tester used their own lab setup and two accounts they control.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Low-rank joint compression: cache one latent, rebuild every head
question: In DeepSeek-V3, which tensors does an MLA layer write to the KV cache for each new token?
options: The per-head keys $k^C$ and values $v^C$
The query latent $c^Q$ and the key latent $c^{KV}$
The layer input $h_t$, since everything can be recomputed from it
The key-value latent $c^{KV}$ and the shared RoPE key $k^R$
explain: Only $c^{KV}$ (512) and $k^R$ (64) are cached. Queries are never cached. Caching $h_t$ (7168 wide) would be larger and would force recomputing projections for every past token.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: MLA in production: kernels, prefill, parallelism, FP8 cache
question: You serve an MLA model on 8 GPUs and KV cache memory is the limit on batch size. Moving attention from 8-way tensor parallelism to 8-way data parallelism (each GPU holds all heads, different requests) mainly helps because:
options: Data parallelism makes the latent smaller
Under tensor parallelism each GPU keeps a full copy of every request's latent cache, so 8 GPUs hold 8 copies; under data parallelism each request's cache lives on one GPU
Tensor parallelism cannot run MLA at all
Data parallelism removes the need for the RoPE key
explain: The latent is shared by all heads, so splitting heads does not split the cache. vLLM documents this 8x duplication for DeepSeek-R1 at TP 8 and offers decode context parallelism as another way to avoid it.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Why serving one model per fine-tune wastes GPUs
question: You host 50 rank-16 all-linear adapters (80 MB each, 16-bit) for one 7B base. How much memory do the adapters take, compared with the base?
options: About 4 GB, under a third of the 13.5 GB base
About 40 GB, three times the base
About 400 MB, negligible
About 675 GB, the same as 50 merged copies
explain: 50 x 80 MB = 4.0 GB. That is real memory, which matters later when adapters compete with the KV cache, but it is small next to 50 x 13.5 GB = 675 GB for merged copies.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Multi-LoRA across GPUs: tensor parallelism for adapters
question: In S-LoRA's scheme, why is the extra communication for rank-16 adapters under 1% of the base's, at any TP degree?
options: Adapters are only applied on GPU 0
The adapter collectives move rank-sized vectors (16 values per token) while the base all-reduces move hidden-size vectors (4,096 values)
LoRA outputs are compressed to 4 bits before sending
Adapters skip the attention block entirely
explain: Each LoRA collective carries the r-dimensional intermediate, and both sides scale with (N - 1)/N, so the ratio is 9r/(4h) per layer: 0.88% at rank 16 for the 7B shape. The last LoRA result is added into the base partial sum and needs no collective of its own.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: The multi-query pipeline: generate, retrieve in parallel, merge
question: You configure LlamaIndex `QueryFusionRetriever(num_queries=4, ...)` with one retriever. How many LLM-generated queries and how many searches does one call make?
options: 4 generated, 4 searches
4 generated, 5 searches
3 generated, 4 searches
1 generated, 4 searches
explain: num_queries counts the original. The prompt asks the LLM for num_queries - 1 = 3 queries, and the original plus those 3 are each searched once per retriever: 4 searches. Setting num_queries=1 disables generation.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: Drift, redundancy, reranker budgets, and when to skip it
question: The LLM sometimes returns phrasings that shift the question to a neighboring topic. Which change most directly limits the damage?
options: Raise N so the drifted phrasing is outvoted
Keep the original query in the set and inspect or filter generated queries that look off-topic
Replace RRF with an unranked union
Drop the original query to avoid bias
explain: The original query cannot drift and anchors fusion. Filtering clearly off-topic rewrites (or constraining the prompt) removes the junk list. Raising N adds cost and may add more drift; a union passes drifted results straight through.

courseTitle: Multi-stage retrieval: designing the retrieve-then-rerank cascade
lessonTitle: LLM listwise reranking and distilling it into cheaper stages
question: RankGPT reranks M = 100 passages with w = 20 and s = 10. You switch to w = 20, s = 5 to give passages more chances to move. How many LLM calls does one pass now make?
explain: ceil((100 - 20) / 5) + 1 = 16 + 1 = 17 calls, reading 17 x 20 = 340 passages. Smaller steps mean more overlap and almost double the cost of s = 10. The guaranteed-correct top also grows, from w - s = 10 to 15.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: Why lookahead helps, and where it does not
question: You have a 7B code model pretrained with 4-token prediction and want the best model for a new coding task. Based on Gloeckle et al.'s CodeContests fine-tuning, what should you try first?
options: Fine-tune with the 4-token loss, since the heads are already trained
Fine-tune a next-token-pretrained model with a 4-token loss instead
Skip fine-tuning; MTP models cannot be fine-tuned
Fine-tune with plain next-token loss after dropping the extra heads
explain: Both ways of fine-tuning the 4-token model beat the next-token baseline, and next-token fine-tuning on top of 4-token pretraining was best overall. Adding a 4-token loss to an already trained next-token model (Llama 2, Table S6) gave no significant gain.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: Reusing the extra heads to decode faster
question: An MTP model with one extra draft has acceptance rate 0.9. Under the simplified independence model, about how many tokens does each forward pass yield, and why is the measured speedup lower?
options: 1.9 tokens; verification passes cost a little more than plain decode steps
2.0 tokens; the draft is always accepted at greedy temperature
1.81 tokens, because 0.9 squared is 0.81
1.9 tokens; the speedup is lower because outputs differ from greedy decoding
explain: Expected tokens = 1 + a = 1.9. The wall-clock gain is smaller because each verifying pass processes extra positions and runs the drafter. Output does not differ: greedy verification reproduces greedy decoding exactly. DeepSeek-V3 reports 85% to 90% acceptance and 1.8x tokens per second.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Why orthogonalize: steepest descent under the spectral norm
question: A weight has 1024 outputs and 4096 inputs. Using the RMS-to-RMS derivation, what factor multiplies $UV^\top$, and what does the reference Muon code use?
options: Derived 0.5, code 1
Derived 2, code 2
Derived 0.5, code 0.5
Derived 1, code 2
explain: The derived factor is $\sqrt{\text{fan-out}/\text{fan-in}} = \sqrt{1024/4096} = 0.5$. The code uses $\sqrt{\max(1, 1024/4096)} = 1$ because it clamps at 1. They agree only for tall matrices.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Muon in a real training stack: parameter groups, sharding and code
question: With ZeRO-1, why does Distributed Muon need an extra collective that distributed AdamW does not?
options: Newton-Schulz needs the full momentum matrix, but each rank only holds a shard of it
Muon's momentum is stored in fp64 and must be broadcast
Muon recomputes gradients on every rank
Muon needs the Hessian, which is sharded across ranks
explain: AdamW's update is elementwise, so a rank can update its shard alone. Orthogonalization mixes all entries of the matrix, so Moonlight adds a bf16 DP gather of the momentum, runs Newton-Schulz on the full matrix and keeps only the local slice.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: Why 'maximal': kernel, mean-field and feature-learning limits
question: Your SP model diverges at width 8192 with the LR tuned at width 512. A colleague proposes dividing the LR by 16, the width ratio, for every layer. What does Tensor Programs IV predict?
options: It is exactly muP
It stays unstable
It becomes stable, but as width keeps growing it drifts into the kernel regime, where features stop learning
It turns the model into the mean-field parametrization
explain: SP with a learning rate of order 1/n is stable but in the kernel regime (Table 1 of the paper). muP differs layer by layer: hidden and input weights get different scalings, and the output layer is initialized smaller, so every layer keeps learning features.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: Verifying a muP implementation, and where muP stops
question: A coord check of your muP Transformer shows the attention logits growing roughly like the square root of width after two steps, while every other curve is flat. What is the most likely bug?
options: Attention still divides q.k by sqrt(d_head) instead of d_head
The base width is too small
Weight decay is not scaled
The learning rate is too small for a coord check
explain: Once q and k become correlated during training, $q^\top k$ grows like $d$, so a $1/\sqrt{d}$ scale leaves logits growing like $\sqrt{d}$ times their target size as heads widen, while the rest of the network is fine. Switching to $1/d$ (or 8/d as in the README) fixes it.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: When spinning wastes the CPU, and how much to spin
question: Your critical sections take about 50 ns, but the machine runs 32 threads on 8 cores. Should you use a pure spin lock in user space?
options: Yes: 50 ns is shorter than any system call
No: with more threads than cores, holders get preempted, and spinners can then burn whole time slices
Yes, as long as the spin loop calls spin_loop()
No: spin locks do not work with more than 8 threads
explain: Short critical sections are only half of the condition. With 32 threads on 8 cores the holder is often not running, and a spinner cannot make it run. A spin-then-sleep mutex handles the short case nearly as well and the preempted case far better.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Why a database keeps old copies of rows
question: Under PostgreSQL MVCC, transaction W runs UPDATE on row R and has not committed yet. Transaction X now runs UPDATE on the same row R. What happens to X?
options: X proceeds immediately and writes its own version next to W's
X waits until W commits or rolls back
X reads W's uncommitted value and overwrites it
X fails instantly with a serialization error
explain: MVCC removes reader versus writer blocking only. Two writers on the same row still conflict, so X waits for W to finish. What X does afterward depends on the isolation level, which lesson 3 covers.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Paying for versions: VACUUM, HOT updates and XID wraparound
question: Autovacuum runs every few minutes on a busy table, yet the table keeps growing and its dead-tuple count never drops. What is the most likely cause?
options: autovacuum_freeze_max_age is set too low
HOT updates are disabled by the fillfactor
A session that opened a transaction hours ago and is still idle in it
The table has too many indexes
explain: Dead tuples are removable only when no snapshot can see them. An old open transaction holds back that horizon for the whole database, so VACUUM runs but has to keep the versions. End the session and the next VACUUM can clean up.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: Scoring whole sequences: transitions and Viterbi by hand
question: Why is the Viterbi table 3 tokens by 3 labels rather than a list of 27 sequence scores?
options: Because the emissions are independent of each other
Because the transition matrix is symmetric, so half the sequences are duplicates
Because the score only couples adjacent labels, so the best prefix ending in a given label can be reused by every extension of it
Because Viterbi is an approximation that prunes low-scoring sequences
explain: A linear-chain model has only bigram interactions (every score term involves at most two adjacent labels), so for each label at each position the single best prefix ending there is all you ever need. Viterbi is exact, not an approximation, and that reuse is what turns an exponential count into n x |Y| x |Y| work.

courseTitle: Nation-state cyber operations and cyber conflict
lessonTitle: Who runs them: services, commands, contractors and fronts
question: DOJ says the Chinese contractor ecosystem produced 'more worldwide computer intrusion victims'. According to the charges, why?
options: Contractors were less skilled, so they were caught more often
Each ministry hired a different contractor for the same target
Contractors only targeted victims outside China, unlike state units
Profit-driven contractors hacked speculatively and sold whatever they found, so they targeted far more broadly than a single tasking would
explain: The release says contractors 'targeted victims speculatively', 'cast a wide net' and sold data, often of no interest to the government, to third parties. Skill and duplicate tasking are not what DOJ describes.

courseTitle: Nation-state cyber operations and cyber conflict
lessonTitle: Attribution by governments: levels, confidence and evidence
question: In the ACH script, why rerun the scoring with only hard-to-fake evidence?
options: Because fakeable evidence is always false and must be deleted
Because ACH requires removing half of the evidence
To make the scores smaller and easier to read
To check that the leading hypothesis does not depend on clues an adversary could plant, such as a persona's claim or language strings
explain: Fakeable items are not necessarily false; they are fragile. If the conclusion survives without them, it is robust to a false flag of the kind Olympic Destroyer used. If it collapses, say so in the brief.

courseTitle: Nation-state cyber operations and cyber conflict
lessonTitle: Wartime cyber in Ukraine, 2022: wipers, a satellite network, the grid
question: ESET said in March 2022 that it had not yet attributed HermeticWiper, while in April it attributed Industroyer2 to Sandworm with high confidence. What best explains the difference?
options: ESET only attributes malware that targets power grids
The government told ESET who wrote Industroyer2
ESET identified Industroyer2 as a new variant of Industroyer, already tied to Sandworm, sharing code with its IEC 104 payload; the new wipers had no such overlap
HermeticWiper was signed, and signed malware cannot be attributed
explain: ESET wrote that the Hermetic families shared no significant code with samples in its collection, while Industroyer2 'shares number of code similarities' with the 2016 tool's IEC 104 payload. Attribution follows evidence, not target type or a signature.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: Why long context needs sparsity, and why bolt-on sparsity disappoints
question: A model uses GQA with 8 query heads per KV group. A sparse method lets each head choose 4 of 64 KV blocks independently, and the heads mostly disagree. During decoding, roughly what happens to memory traffic per group?
options: It drops to 4/64 of dense, since each head reads 4 blocks
It drops to somewhere up to 32/64 of dense, because the union of the heads' picks must be loaded
It is unchanged, because sparse methods never reduce memory reads
It increases, because sparse methods must read all keys to score them
explain: Heads in a GQA group share one KV cache, so the kernel loads the union of their selections: up to 8 x 4 = 32 distinct blocks. Compute per head is 4/64, but decoding is memory bound, so the union is what sets latency. This is exactly why NSA forces one shared selection per group.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: DeepSeek Sparse Attention: a lightning indexer picks tokens
question: During DSA's dense warm-up, what is the indexer trained to predict?
options: The next token, using the language modeling loss
Which tokens NSA's compression branch would select
The main attention distribution for each query, summed over heads and L1-normalized, via a KL loss
A binary label for whether each token is in the top 2048
explain: The target $p_{t,:}$ is the dense main attention summed over heads and normalized. The indexer's softmax is pulled toward it with KL divergence while the main model is frozen, so the indexer learns which tokens the model actually attends to before sparsity is switched on.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: Why MD5 misses copies, and the average hash that does not
question: Why does aHash squash the image to 8x8 without keeping the aspect ratio?
options: So that the hash fits in a 64-bit integer, which is the only reason
Because grayscale conversion only works on square images
To keep high-frequency detail that distinguishes near copies
So that a resized or stretched copy reduces to nearly the same 64 pixels and therefore the same bits
explain: The shrink is what makes the hash scale-invariant: every size and aspect ratio of the same picture is crushed to the same 8x8 grid. It also discards high frequencies on purpose, the opposite of the last option.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: PDQ, learned copy detectors and building a real pipeline
question: Why does PDQ use 256 bits where pHash uses 64?
options: 256-bit integers are faster to XOR
More bits keep unrelated images far apart even in web-scale collections, where a 64-bit hash with a useful threshold yields many chance matches
The DCT requires 256 outputs
To store the image's color histogram
explain: With 64 bits and threshold 10, uniform random hashes already give about 10 chance candidates per query in a billion images. With 256 bits and threshold 31, the random-collision rate is astronomically small; the PDQ authors call 256 bits appropriate for web scale.

courseTitle: NeMo RL: NVIDIA's Ray-based post-training library
lessonTitle: Training backends (Automodel, Megatron) and generation backends
question: A multi-node Megatron run crashes on node 2 because it cannot find the converted checkpoint that node 1 created. What is the documented fix?
options: Set force_reconvert_from_hf: true on every step
Switch to the Automodel backend
Point NRL_MEGATRON_CHECKPOINT_DIR (or HF_HOME) at shared storage visible to all nodes
Lower gpu_memory_utilization
explain: The converted Megatron checkpoint directory must be accessible from all nodes, for example on NFS (Network File System, a shared disk that every node mounts). The docs recommend a shared HF_HOME, which yields HF_HOME/nemo_rl.

courseTitle: NeMo RL: NVIDIA's Ray-based post-training library
lessonTitle: SFT, DPO and distillation on the same machinery
question: A colleague trains SFT on multi-turn tutoring logs and sees the model imitate the tutor's early clarifying questions, which they only meant as context. Which switch matches their intent?
options: sft.only_unmask_final: true, so only the last assistant message is trained
tokenizer.chat_template: null, so the template stops marking assistant turns
policy.sequence_packing.enabled: true, so each turn becomes its own sequence
dpo.sft_loss_weight: 0.1, so imitation is down-weighted
explain: add_loss_mask_to_message_log masks in every assistant message by default; only_unmask_final keeps the mask on the final message alone (7 of 52 tokens in the example). A passthrough template changes rendering, not masking.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: VLANs, VLAN hopping and 802.1X port authentication
question: A trunk's native VLAN is 1 and the guest Wi-Fi bridge is also on VLAN 1. Which change best removes the double-tagging risk?
options: Add more VLANs
Turn on DHCP snooping
Give the trunk a native VLAN that no user or guest port uses
Move the payment terminals to VLAN 2
explain: Double tagging needs the sender to be on the trunk's native VLAN, because that is the tag the first switch strips. Making the native VLAN one with no user ports removes the precondition. The other options do not touch the tag handling.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: BGP hijacks and route leaks: the MyEtherWallet case
question: An AS announces 205.251.192.0/24 while the owner announces 205.251.192.0/23. Where accepted, which wins, and why?
options: The /24, because routers choose the longest (most specific) matching prefix
Neither: routers drop overlapping prefixes
Whichever has the shorter AS path
The /23, because it was announced first
explain: Longest prefix match is applied before any BGP preference between routes: a /24 is more specific than a /23, so destinations inside it follow the /24. AS path length only decides between announcements of the same prefix.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: DDoS: three classes, and the maths of amplification
question: At 17:26 GitHub withdrew its BGP announcements from its transit providers and announced its prefixes only through Akamai. Why did that relieve GitHub's own links?
options: It changed GitHub's IP addresses, so the reflectors lost their target
BGP withdrawal blocks UDP traffic everywhere on the internet
Traffic for GitHub's prefixes now followed routes into Akamai's much larger edge, where filters dropped the flood before it reached GitHub
Akamai asked the memcached servers to stop answering
explain: BGP decides which networks carry traffic toward a prefix. Announcing only via Akamai made every packet for GitHub, attack included, enter through Akamai, whose capacity absorbed 1.35 Tbps and whose access control lists dropped the memcached responses. The addresses and the reflectors did not change.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: Segmentation, zero trust and the Target breach
question: Which statement matches NIST SP 800-207's idea of zero trust?
options: Every access request is authenticated and authorised per session, using policy that includes device state, regardless of where on the network it comes from
Devices inside the corporate network are trusted; outside ones are not
Once a user logs in to the VPN, they may access any internal system
Zero trust means blocking all traffic
explain: Zero trust removes implicit trust from network location. The log-in-to-the-VPN model is exactly the implicit trust zone it replaces. It does not mean blocking everything, but deciding each session explicitly.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Inside a pcap file: headers, snap length, timestamps and integrity
question: A colleague's capture tool writes timestamps in nanoseconds. Which field tells a pcap reader to interpret the second time field as nanoseconds rather than microseconds?
options: The link-layer type
The snapshot length
The magic number
The version number
explain: The pcap-savefile manual says the magic number 0xa1b23c4d (instead of 0xa1b2c3d4) marks a file whose packet timestamps are seconds and nanoseconds. The magic number also reveals the writer's byte order.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Zeek's protocol logs and pivoting with uid, fuid and Community ID
question: An analyst has an ssl.log line for a suspicious TLS 1.3 connection and searches x509.log for its certificate, but finds nothing. Why?
options: Zeek never logs certificates
The certificate is in files.log instead
TLS 1.3 encrypts the server's certificate, so a passive sensor cannot see it unless traffic is decrypted
x509.log only records client certificates
explain: Zeek's ssl.log documentation shows that with TLS 1.3 there is no certificate information, because the Certificate message is sent after the handshake keys are set. With TLS 1.2 the certificate crosses in clear text and appears in x509.log. The server name (SNI) is still visible unless Encrypted Client Hello is used.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Case: hunting Cobalt Strike servers by certificate, JARM and quirks
question: x509.log shows a certificate with serial 08BB00EE on a connection from a finance workstation to an unfamiliar internet address. What is the best next step?
options: Ignore it: certificate serials are random
Block the whole /8 network immediately and close the case
Treat it as a strong lead: list its connections via ssl.log (x509.log has no uid), check other hosts using that address, and seek corroboration such as port 50050 or a recent first-seen date
Re-image every machine in the company
explain: 0x08BB00EE is 146473198, the default Cobalt Strike certificate serial that Recorded Future called the surest single method. A red-team exercise or a researcher's server could also present it, so you confirm with the connection's behaviour and other hosts' contact with the address before escalating. Blind mass actions without scoping are not a response plan.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Network forensics for incident response: a worked IcedID investigation
question: Which single filter would most quickly show the infected host's first contact with attacker infrastructure in the IcedID pcap?
options: tcp.flags.syn == 1
dns.qry.name contains "microsoft"
http.request with the clients' subnet, looking for requests addressed to a bare IP
tls.handshake.type == 2
explain: Unit 42 starts with a basic web filter and looks for unencrypted HTTP to an IP address without a domain, which revealed GET /main.php at 15:31:08. SYN packets alone show every connection, ServerHellos (type 2) show every TLS session, and a Microsoft name filter targets nothing in this chain.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: IP addresses, subnets and CIDR
question: An alert says traffic came from 172.32.8.9 and an analyst writes 'internal host, private range'. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, all 172.x.x.x addresses are private
172.32.8.9 is outside 172.16.0.0/12 (which ends at 172.31.255.255), so it is a public address
Private ranges only exist in IPv6
Only 192.168.0.0/16 is private
explain: The /12 means the first 12 bits are fixed: 172.16 through 172.31. 172.32 is the first value outside it. Misreading private ranges is a classic triage mistake: it can make an external attacker look like an internal machine, or the reverse.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: UDP and ICMP: no handshake, and messages about the network
question: Why are amplification attacks built on UDP services rather than TCP services?
options: UDP is always faster than TCP
UDP servers are usually unpatched
TCP traffic is encrypted, UDP is not
A single forged UDP datagram is a whole request, so the server replies to the forged address; TCP needs a handshake the spoofer cannot complete
explain: The handshake is TCP's accidental anti-spoofing check: the SYN-ACK goes to the real owner of the forged address and nothing further happens. UDP has no such step, so any server that answers a small UDP request with a big reply is a potential amplifier.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: Reading a packet capture like a defender
question: In Wireshark you want only packets where a host tries to open a TCP connection. Which display filter is right?
options: tcp port 80
tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0
tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0
tcp.flags.reset == 1
explain: A connection attempt is the first handshake segment: SYN set, ACK not set. `tcp port 80` and the `tcp[tcpflags]` expression are capture filter (pcap-filter) syntax, not display filter syntax, and the `tcp[tcpflags]` one would also match SYN-ACKs. Resets are a different event.
